items.question: What is NowBuild?
items.answer: NowBuild is an AI Marketing Agent Team for solo founders who have built a product but do not know how to grow or validate its market. The team shares product memory, calls professional Channel Skills, and continuously researches, creates, distributes, and reviews one 30-day campaign using real market feedback.

items.question: How is this different from ChatGPT?
items.answer: ChatGPT is useful for one-off answers or drafts. NowBuild coordinates multiple Agents that share product memory, a market hypothesis, channel plans, publishing progress, and real feedback while calling Channel Skills to keep the same campaign moving.

items.question: What are Channel Skills?
items.answer: Channel Skills are platform-specific execution playbooks. A Reddit Agent studies community context and real questions; a TikTok Agent prepares hooks, spoken scripts, and storyboards; an SEO Agent organizes keywords and content clusters around search intent. They share one market goal but never simply rewrite the same post everywhere.

items.question: Can NowBuild publish completely automatically?
items.answer: NowBuild prepares publish-ready work and assists with browser publishing where the platform allows it. Login, CAPTCHA, account authorization, media selection, community-rule checks, and final confirmation may still require you. NowBuild does not store your platform passwords or pretend those platform controls do not exist.

items.question: How do automated Directory submissions work?
items.answer: The Directory Agent first matches opportunities by product type, audience, and submission requirements. It then prepares descriptions, tags, assets, and form fields and executes supported submission flows. Each third-party platform still controls acceptance, timing, fees, and whether a backlink is provided.

items.question: Can 30 days guarantee users or revenue?
items.answer: No. NowBuild promises a continuous, recorded, reviewable market-validation process—not guaranteed traffic, rankings, users, or revenue. After 30 days, you should have channel performance, user response, reusable content, and the market signals needed for the next decision.

posts.title: The Product Is Done. Now What? A 30-Day Roadmap for Your First Launch
posts.excerpt: Most builders don't get stuck on the product — they get stuck on the step after shipping. Here's a day-1-to-day-30 market action roadmap.
posts.author: NowBuild Team
posts.content:
When the product is ready, the next step is not a single launch announcement. Run a 30-day sequence that moves from positioning and audience research to conversations, useful content, focused distribution, and a review of what produced qualified users. Each week should answer a different question, and each day should create evidence for the next decision.

A first launch is successful when it reduces uncertainty. You should finish the month knowing more about who needs the product, which message they understand, where you can reach them, what prevents activation, and which actions are worth repeating.

## Before day 1: Define the result you want

Choose one primary outcome for the 30 days. It might be activated users, completed demos, qualified waitlist signups, repository usage, or customer interviews. Avoid combining awareness, revenue, community growth, and every channel metric into one goal. A focused outcome makes it possible to judge whether an action helped.

Define the activation event as well. A signup is not necessarily a user: decide what someone must complete to experience the product's first meaningful value. Then make sure you can record the source, signup, activation, and useful feedback without building a complicated reporting system.

## Days 1–3: Build a launch brief from evidence

Write a short source of truth for the campaign. It should explain what the product does, who it is for, the problem it solves, the alternatives users have today, the main difference, the activation event, and any claims that still need verification. Use product behavior, customer conversations, support questions, competitor pages, and public discussions as evidence.

Keep uncertain assumptions visible. If you do not yet know whether a segment cares about the problem, label it as a hypothesis instead of turning it into confident landing-page copy. The brief should prevent different channels from inventing different versions of the product.

## Days 4–7: Choose a position and two channel jobs

Turn the brief into one clear promise: for a specific audience, the product helps create a specific result through a mechanism or trade-off that matters. Test the promise against the landing page, onboarding, and product experience. If those surfaces tell different stories, fix the gap before increasing distribution.

Choose one primary channel for reaching the audience and one supporting channel with a different job. For example, a community may create conversations while a guide captures search demand; founder content may create discovery while email or a landing page captures intent. Do not open many channels that all repeat the same announcement.

## Week 2: Start with conversations, not volume

Contact a small number of relevant people, participate in one suitable community, and publish one problem-led or founder-led piece. Ask about the current workflow, the cost of the problem, what they have tried, and what would make a new solution credible. Show the product only when it is relevant to the conversation.

Record the language people use, the objections they repeat, the alternatives they mention, and the point where interest stops. These observations are more useful than generic engagement because they tell you what to change in the message, onboarding, or product.

## Week 2 review: Diagnose the first conversion path

Review the path from qualified attention to product visit, signup, activation, and follow-up use. If content gets attention but no visits, its connection to the product may be weak. If people visit but do not sign up, the audience or promise may be wrong. If they sign up but do not activate, repair onboarding or the product experience before chasing more traffic.

Choose one message to keep, one friction point to fix, and one channel action to repeat. Do not rewrite everything at once; otherwise the next result will not tell you which change mattered.

## Week 3: Turn real questions into a content system

Build content from the questions collected in the first two weeks. Create one substantial guide, demonstration, comparison, case note, or workflow that answers a real decision. Break it into smaller channel-native pieces only when each version fits the platform: a community answer should be complete, a short video needs a visual mechanism, and a social post needs one clear observation rather than a compressed article.

Connect the pieces with internal links and a consistent next step. Someone who discovers a guide should be able to understand the product, inspect how it works, and try the relevant workflow without searching the site.

## Week 3 distribution: Add focused launch surfaces

Submit the product to directories and launch platforms that match its category, audience, geography, and requirements. Prepare consistent descriptions, screenshots, tags, and founder details, then track submitted, under-review, published, rejected, and follow-up states. A listing is distribution infrastructure, not proof of demand.

Reuse only what remains accurate across platforms. Adapt the title, context, proof, and call to action to the destination instead of pasting the same launch copy everywhere. Respect community rules and keep final publishing, payments, verification, and account access under human control.

## Week 4: Concentrate the launch around evidence

Use the strongest message and the clearest product demonstration for a coordinated launch moment. Update the landing page, publish the main story or guide, contact people who previously showed intent, and distribute to the selected channels. The goal is not to manufacture noise; it is to make the best-supported version of the product easy to discover and evaluate.

Continue answering questions after publishing. Replies, objections, setup problems, and reasons people share the product are part of the launch data, not interruptions to the campaign.

## Days 27–30: Review what should continue

Separate activity from outcomes. Count qualified conversations, product visits, signups, activations, retained use, directory publications, and useful feedback. Compare channels by the quality of users and learning they produced, not only by reach. A small source of activated users may deserve more attention than a large source of passive views.

Decide what to continue, change, pause, or test next. Keep the channel and message combinations that produced qualified movement, repair the largest conversion gap, and turn unresolved questions into the next content and product backlog.

## Use a simple daily operating loop

Each day, review the current goal and yesterday's evidence, complete one focused action, record what happened, and prepare the next step. A useful action might be one customer conversation, one thorough community answer, a landing-page improvement, a directory batch, or a content section based on a real objection.

The plan should change when evidence changes. It should not change merely because a post had low likes or because a different platform became fashionable. Use a weekly review to make larger decisions so daily noise does not constantly reset the strategy.

## What should you measure during a first launch?

Track a small funnel: qualified attention, product visits, signups, activation, and continued use. Add qualitative evidence such as repeated phrases, objections, requested use cases, support friction, and reasons people decline. These signals explain the numbers and help determine whether the next change belongs in acquisition, positioning, onboarding, or the product itself.

Avoid invented benchmarks. The useful comparison is between your own channels, messages, and weekly experiments under similar conditions.

## Common mistakes that weaken a 30-day launch

Launching on every channel at once creates activity without clean learning. Changing the audience and message every few days prevents a fair test. Treating likes as demand hides the gap between attention and activation. Publishing claims without evidence damages trust. Writing many shallow articles creates pages without a clear job. Automating account actions without review creates platform and brand risk.

A good launch is narrower: one audience hypothesis, one primary outcome, one shared product truth, a small number of channel jobs, and a fixed review rhythm.

## Should you wait until the product is perfect?

Wait until a suitable user can reach the core value and you can support them through obvious failures. Do not wait for every feature or edge case. Launching with known limitations is acceptable when those limits are stated clearly and the product does not create material risk for the user.

## How many channels should a solo founder use?

Start with one primary acquisition channel and one supporting surface. Add another only when it has a distinct job and the existing workflow is sustainable. The right number depends on production effort, audience access, and how quickly you can learn—not on a universal launch checklist.

## What happens after day 30?

A 30-day campaign should end with a continuation decision, not silence. Keep the strongest channel, message, and content assets; fix the largest activation or conversion problem; archive unsupported assumptions; and plan the next month around the evidence you now have.

posts.title: How to Choose Your First Marketing Channel, by Product Type
posts.excerpt: Product Hunt, Twitter, Reddit, newsletters… too many channels is a first-time marketer's worst enemy. Here's how to subtract.
posts.author: NowBuild Team
posts.content:
Choose your first marketing channel by matching one reachable audience, one action you want that audience to take, and one format you can produce consistently. Product type narrows the options, but it does not determine the winner. Select one primary channel, run a bounded test, and keep it only when qualified people move toward product value.

The best first channel is rarely the largest platform. It is the place where you can observe the right problem, contribute credibly, connect attention to a clear next step, and learn quickly enough to improve the next attempt.

## Start with the outcome, not the platform

Define the result the channel should create. Early goals might include qualified conversations, demo requests, activated users, repository adoption, newsletter signups, or customer interviews. A community can create conversations, search content can capture existing intent, and a launch platform can concentrate discovery, but none automatically completes the full conversion path.

Choose one primary outcome and one activation event. This prevents you from judging a channel only by the metric it makes easiest to see.

## Describe one reachable audience

Write a narrow audience hypothesis: who experiences the problem, what situation makes it urgent, what they use today, and where you can observe them discussing it. Startup founders is usually too broad. Solo SaaS founders preparing their first public launch creates clearer places, questions, and content ideas to test.

Audience access includes more than platform size. Consider whether the relevant people are active, whether you can identify their questions, whether the rules allow useful participation, and whether you have enough credibility to contribute.

## Map the complete conversion path

For each candidate channel, write the path from discovery to activation. Someone may see a post, visit a profile, click a guide, reach a product page, sign up, and complete the first useful workflow. Every additional step can lose intent. Make the next action clear and ensure the landing page continues the same promise as the channel content.

If a platform does not allow links or promotion, decide whether its job is trust, research, or relationships rather than direct acquisition. A channel can still be valuable, but it should be measured against the job it actually performs.

## Give every channel one job

Direct outreach is good for targeted conversations. Communities expose real questions and objections. Search content answers persistent intent. Founder-led social content creates repeated discovery and trust. Video demonstrates mechanisms that are easier to see than describe. Email follows up with people who already showed interest. Product directories and launch platforms create structured discovery and references.

The same channel can play different roles for different products. State the role before choosing the content format or posting cadence.

## Build a shortlist by product type

For a consumer product, examine visual, story-led, search, or community surfaces where people already share the relevant behavior. For a B2B tool, compare direct outreach, professional communities, founder content, integration ecosystems, partner audiences, and high-intent search questions. For a developer product, make documentation and the first technical outcome clear before testing developer communities, GitHub, technical publishing, or search.

For an open-source project, the README, examples, installation path, and maintainer responsiveness are part of the channel. For a local service, local search, referrals, partnerships, and trusted community groups may matter more than global launch platforms. For a course or consulting offer, choose surfaces where expertise can be demonstrated through useful long-form material, workshops, or direct conversations.

These are hypotheses, not guaranteed channel assignments. Verify actual audience presence and platform rules before committing.

## Score the candidates before you start

Give each candidate a simple 1–3 score for audience access, fit with the desired action, founder credibility, format fit, production effort, feedback speed, and ability to track the next step. Write one sentence explaining every score so the decision does not become arbitrary.

Prefer the channel with the strongest overall learning path, not necessarily the highest theoretical reach. If two options are close, choose the one you can test with less time and clearer evidence.

## Check whether the format is sustainable

A channel is not a fit if its required format cannot be produced at useful quality. A founder who can explain technical decisions may sustain written tutorials but struggle with daily visual production. Another founder may demonstrate a consumer workflow naturally through short video but find long-form writing too slow.

Choose a minimum sustainable cadence and estimate the full cost: research, production, review, publishing, replies, and measurement. Do not count only the time required to draft the first post.

## Design a two-week channel test

Use one audience, one landing-page promise, one primary channel, and one review date. Decide in advance what you can realistically complete: personal conversations, useful community contributions, demonstrations, guides, or posts. Keep the message stable enough to learn while adapting each contribution to its context.

Record qualified replies, profile or product visits, signups, activation, and useful objections. For search content, two weeks is usually too short to judge ranking potential, so use early crawl, indexing, and engagement evidence while continuing to evaluate over a longer window.

## Diagnose the result instead of declaring victory or failure

If the right people respond but do not visit, the connection between content and product may be unclear. If they visit but do not sign up, the promise, audience, or perceived cost may be wrong. If they sign up but do not activate, the channel may be working while onboarding or product value is failing. If the intended audience never appears, revisit the channel or audience hypothesis.

Make one major adjustment at a time. Changing the audience, promise, format, landing page, and cadence together makes the next result difficult to interpret.

## When should you keep, adjust, or pause a channel?

Keep the channel when qualified people progress to the next step, the work is repeatable, and the audience continues to produce relevant questions. Adjust it when the right people engage but the format or next step underperforms. Pause it when the intended audience is absent, the rules make participation unsuitable, the production burden is unsustainable, or repeated tests create activity without qualified movement.

A pause is not permanent failure. Save what you learned and revisit the channel when the product, audience, proof, or operating capacity changes.

## Add a second channel only when it has a different job

A supporting channel should complete the path rather than duplicate it. Search content may capture intent created by community conversations. Email may follow up with people who discovered a founder post. A product directory may add structured discovery while direct outreach generates feedback.

If both channels require the same content and compete for the same limited time, keep one until the workflow becomes sustainable.

## Avoid common first-channel mistakes

Do not choose a platform only because another founder grew there. Do not copy one announcement across every network. Do not treat followers, likes, or raw traffic as proof of product demand. Do not ignore community rules. Do not automate conversations that depend on trust and context. Do not keep publishing when signups repeatedly fail to activate.

The purpose of the first channel is learning and repeatability, not appearing active everywhere.

## What if no channel produces results?

Return to the audience, problem, promise, and activation path before adding more platforms. Interview people who declined, inspect where the conversion path stops, compare how they describe the problem, and confirm that the product creates a meaningful first outcome. More distribution cannot repair a weak or unclear value path by itself.

## How long should you test a channel?

Use enough time to complete a meaningful number of actions and observe the next step. Direct outreach and communities can often produce learning within days or weeks; search, partnerships, and audience-building usually need longer. Set the review window according to the channel's mechanism instead of forcing every channel into the same deadline.

## Can SEO be the first marketing channel?

Yes, when users already search for a specific problem, you can answer it with credible depth, and the business can wait for slower compounding discovery. Pair it with conversations or community research so the early content uses real customer language. SEO is a weaker first choice when the category is unknown, the problem is not searched, or immediate feedback is essential.

posts.title: How to Get Your First 100 Users Without Spending a Dollar on Ads
posts.excerpt: Paid ads can amplify an untested message during a first launch. Here are three zero-budget paths for finding your first 100 users.
posts.author: NowBuild Team
posts.content:
You can find your first 100 users without paid ads by combining personal outreach, useful participation in existing communities, founder-led content, product launch directories, and search content that answers a narrow problem. The goal is not to appear everywhere. It is to create enough qualified conversations to learn who activates, why they stay, and which repeatable path brings in the next user.

Treat 100 as a learning milestone rather than a promise or a vanity target. Ten people who use the core workflow and explain what helped them are more valuable than a hundred unqualified signups who never return.

## Decide what counts as a real user

Define one activation event before you start outreach. For a writing tool it might be publishing a first document; for a developer product, completing an integration; for a marketplace, creating a usable listing. A signup is only the beginning. Your acquisition work should be judged by how many suitable people reach the first meaningful outcome.

Write down the audience, the problem they already recognize, the activation event, and the easiest way to give feedback. This keeps every post, reply, and conversation connected to the same learning goal.

## Prepare the shortest credible path to value

Before looking for traffic, make sure a new visitor can understand who the product is for, what result it helps create, and what to do next. Remove onboarding steps that are not required for the first useful outcome. Add a simple way to contact you, and record the source of each signup so you can connect activation and feedback to the action that produced them.

You do not need a complex analytics stack. A small log with the date, channel, message, visits, signups, activations, and useful replies is enough to compare early experiments.

## Path 1: Start with people you can contact personally

Build a small list of people who plausibly experience the problem: former colleagues, customers from related work, people who asked a relevant question, or users frustrated with an alternative. Relevance matters more than list size. Do not scrape a large audience and send the same pitch to everyone.

A useful first message has four parts: the reason you chose this person, the problem you are exploring, a brief explanation of what you built, and a low-pressure request. Ask whether the problem is real for them before asking for a signup. When someone declines, record the reason instead of trying to overcome every objection.

## Path 2: Publish the founder story behind the product

A founder story works when it helps the reader recognize a problem, not when it turns into a biography. Explain the moment you noticed the problem, the workaround you tried, the trade-off you rejected, and what your product now does differently. Include screenshots or a short demonstration when they make the mechanism easier to understand.

Publish the story where you already have context or relationships, then compare it with a practical tutorial or problem-focused post. Track qualified replies, profile visits, product visits, and activations. Likes alone cannot tell you whether the message reached likely users.

## Path 3: Help in communities where the problem is discussed

Look for communities in which people already ask about the problem: a focused subreddit, a Slack or Discord group, Hacker News, Indie Hackers, a professional forum, or a local-language community. Read the rules and recent conversations before contributing. Some communities welcome product feedback; others allow only educational participation or prohibit promotion entirely.

Answer the question in full even if nobody clicks. Mention your product only when it is directly relevant, disclose that you built it, and explain its limitations. Repeated useful participation builds more trust than dropping the same launch link into many communities.

## Path 4: Use launch platforms and product directories selectively

Directories can create discovery, backlinks, and launch-day attention, but not every listing reaches the same audience. Choose platforms by product category, geography, pricing, and submission requirements. Prepare a consistent product name, URL, one-sentence promise, longer description, screenshots, founder details, and category tags before submitting.

Track submitted, under-review, published, rejected, and follow-up states separately. A published listing is distribution infrastructure, not proof of demand. Judge it by qualified referral visits and activated users over time.

## Path 5: Answer one search question better than the alternatives

Search content is slower than direct outreach, but it can keep bringing the right problem to your site. Start with a narrow question you heard in real conversations. Give the direct answer first, show the decision process or workflow, include an example, and link naturally to the product only where it helps complete the task.

One useful guide connected to a product page is a better starting point than many short articles targeting loosely related keywords. Update the guide when customer questions reveal missing steps or unclear language.

## Turn the five paths into a 30-day plan

In week one, define activation, fix the shortest onboarding path, contact a small number of relevant people, and publish one clear founder or problem story. In week two, participate in one or two suitable communities and submit the product to a focused directory batch. In week three, publish a practical guide based on the questions and objections collected so far. In week four, repeat the strongest action, follow up with people who showed intent, and review the complete path from discovery to activation.

Keep the workload sustainable. One thoughtful community answer, a few personal conversations, or one useful content improvement can be enough for a day. The purpose of the schedule is consistent learning, not filling every channel with content.

## Measure the path, not just the signup count

Review four stages: qualified attention, product visits, signups, and activation. If people engage with a post but do not visit, the connection to the product may be unclear. If they visit but do not sign up, the audience or landing-page promise may be wrong. If they sign up but do not activate, acquisition is not the first problem to solve; onboarding or product value needs attention.

Keep qualitative evidence beside the numbers. Save recurring phrases, objections, use cases, and reasons people decline. Those details should shape the next landing-page revision, content topic, and outreach message.

## When should you consider paid ads?

Consider a small paid test after you can identify a reachable audience, a message that produces qualified interest, an activation event, and a reason activated users continue. Paid acquisition can then test whether a known path scales. Before those pieces exist, ads often make it harder to separate a targeting problem from a message, onboarding, or product problem.

## What if you have no existing audience?

Start with observable conversations rather than follower count. Interview people in your extended network, answer existing questions, study reviews of alternatives, and participate in one focused community. An audience can be built from repeated relevance; it does not need to exist before the first useful conversation.

## Should you offer free access?

Free access can reduce friction when the user can reach value quickly and the cost of serving them is manageable. It does not replace a clear audience or activation path. If you offer a free plan or trial, ask for feedback at a meaningful moment and distinguish active evaluators from accounts that never begin.

## What should you do after the first 100 users?

Separate activated and retained users from inactive signups, identify the acquisition path that produced the strongest users, and keep the message that best describes their problem. Continue the repeatable path, repair the largest conversion drop, and use the questions you collected to plan the next content and product improvements.

About.title: About NowBuild
About.subtitle: NowBuild exists to help individuals turn a finished software product into a market—and a market into a complete business loop.

story.title: Our Story
story.content: AI made shipping a product easier than ever — you can launch an MVP over a weekend. But we kept seeing builders stuck at the next step: product done, a few posts shared, 12 visitors in 7 days, zero signups, and no idea what to do tomorrow. The problem isn't that they lack theory. It's that nobody connected strategy → daily action → market feedback → strategy evolution into a path you actually want to open every day. That's why we built NowBuild (nowbuild.ai): strategy through conversation, execution driven by a calendar, content pre-drafted by AI, and reviews that evolve the plan.

mission.title: Our Mission
mission.content: Enable individuals to complete the whole loop: build a useful product, build a market through sustained conversation and evidence, then build a business that can keep moving without a large team.

items.title: Execution over theory
items.description: Builders don't lack growth articles — they lack 'what exactly to post today'. We deliver daily actions, not another GTM course.

items.title: You review, you publish
items.description: AI drafts 80%, but the voice facing the market is always yours. We reduce friction; we don't run your accounts.

items.title: Honest promises
items.description: We promise a system and a rhythm, not a guaranteed user count. You'll have reviewable market feedback within the first week.

items.title: Small and deep
items.description: No all-in-one startup suite. We do one thing extremely well: your first 30 days of taking a product to market.

cta.title: Ready to build your business loop?
cta.description: Start with the complete 30-day Market Strategy Report free, then decide whether to put your Launch Team to work.
